What it remembers

Every phrase is stored as the set of Kenyon cells it lit up. The number on the right is read straight off those cells' synapses, so it only moves when someone actually teaches it something.

said to ittimesapproach

Teach it to talk

Give it a phrase to recognise and a thing to say back. It smells the phrase three times, and the Kenyon cells that fire become the handle for that reply. One lesson is usually enough.

The reply can carry live values, filled in from the brain each time:
{looking} what it is watching · {mood} how it is · {feeling} what it makes of the smell · {times} times smelled · {turn} which way it turned · {state} its state · {cells} Kenyon cells · {spikes} spikes ·
{linked} words it links to this smell · {reminds} what it was reminded of
e.g. Not now. I am watching {looking}.

The words are yours. Which one comes out is its own doing.

Paste a whole lot at once

One per line, what it hears,what it says. Wrap a field in quotes if it contains a comma. Roughly three seconds each, so a hundred and fifty takes about seven minutes — leave the tab open.

hearssays

Name its states

These are patterns of output the fly fell into by itself. Nothing here was designed — a pattern unlike any before became a new one, and familiar ones have been averaging together ever since. Measured, its output supports about five it can hold apart, so the list stops at eight.

Give one a sentence and it will say that whenever it lands there. The same live values work here — {looking}, {mood}, {times} and the rest.

statetimessays

Give it a voice

The brain decides everything — how wary it is, what it was reminded of, what it was taught to feel. A language model only finds the words. It is never shown your message, because the fly cannot read it either.

checking for WebGPU…

Downloads once and stays in the browser cache. No key, no server, no cost.

What this needs

WebGPU, which means a recent Chrome, Edge or Safari on a desktop. Most phones cannot do it, and those visitors fall back to taught phrases on their own.

The first load pulls the model down — minutes on a slow connection — then it is cached and instant. It shares the graphics card with the brain, so drop the speed slider if things get choppy.

To switch it on for everyone, set VOICE.local near the top of the file to the model id.

A server holding the key. Also the way to use a model running on your own machine — an Ollama URL works here and is detected automatically.

Nothing set.

A Cloudflare Worker, if you want one 
export default {
  async fetch(req, env) {
    if (req.method !== "POST") return new Response("POST only", {status: 405});
    const r = await fetch("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        "x-api-key": env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
        "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01"
      },
      body: await req.text()
    });
    return new Response(r.body, {
      status: r.status,
      headers: {"content-type": "application/json",
                "access-control-allow-origin": "*"}
    });
  }
}

Never put a key in this file — it is downloaded by everyone who opens the page.

The shared brain

Paste the snippet Firebase gave you — the whole thing, straight from the console. It will pull the fields out itself.

Not connected. It is learning in this browser only.

Make it shared for everyone, not just this browser

Connecting here only affects your machine. For visitors to join the same fly, the config has to live in the file. Open fly-brain.html, find FIREBASE_CONFIG near the top of the first script, and replace null with the block below.

Then in Firebase, open Realtime Database → Rules and set:

{ "rules": { "fly": { ".read": true, ".write": true } } }

That lets anyone read and write the fly. Export the fly node now and then so a bad day can be undone.
